title: The Selection Rule for the Rigid Rotor
lead: Light drives a transition through the transition dipole between two states, and a selection rule says when that dipole is not zero. For a rotating molecule the question comes down to an integral of two spherical harmonics.
notes: Shared under CC BY-SA 4.0, the licence of the page it is adapted from; the book's pull-quote repeating the sentence before it is kept as a note.
exercise_notes: The one exercise was written by AI with an AI solution; its Bloom level and concept tags were chosen by AI.

exercises.source_id: This leads to the selection rule
exercises.prompt: A heteronuclear diatomic molecule in the rotational state $J = 1$, $M = 0$ absorbs or emits z-polarized microwave radiation. Which states can it reach?

answer.hint: Apply $\Delta M = 0$ and $\Delta J = \pm 1$ together, in both directions.
answer.solution: For z-polarized light the $\varphi$ integral keeps only $M' = M$, so $M$ stays 0, and the recurrence keeps only $J' = J \pm 1$, so $J$ goes to 2 in absorption or to 0 in emission. $J = 3$ would need $\Delta J = 2$, and $M = \pm 1$ would need $\Delta M = \pm 1$; both integrals vanish. All of this assumes the gross selection rule is met: the transition moment carries the factor $\mu$, so HCl, with a permanent dipole moment, has a rotational spectrum, while N₂, whose dipole moment is zero, has none however its $J$ and $M$ change.

footnotes.html: A selection rule says when the probability of a transition can be non-zero.
“m” is $\mu$, the permanent dipole moment, which stands in front of the integral.
This page has no section on electronic transitions; the one-electron rules $\Delta l = \pm 1$ are in Section 8.11.

derivations.what: the selection rules of the rigid rotor
derivations.source: Physical Chemistry (LibreTexts), 13.12 The Selection Rule for the Rigid Rotor

assumes.text: The rotor's dipole $\kmud$ lies along its axis, so its component along the field is $\kmuz = \kmud\cos\ktheta$.

steps.cap: $N_{JM}$ is a normalization constant. The conjugate of $e^{iM'\varphi}$ is $e^{-iM'\varphi}$, so the two phases combine into $e^{i(M-M')\varphi}$.
The standard substitution: with $x = \cos\theta$, $dx = -\sin\theta\,d\theta$, and the limits $0$ and $\pi$ become $1$ and $-1$.

nodes.note: The book's integrand lacks the conjugate on $Y_{J'}^{M'}$, and after the substitution it drops the $x$ that $\mu_z = \mu\cos\theta$ brings; it also prints $e^{I(M-M')\phi}$ for $e^{i(M-M')\phi}$ and $x = \cos q$ for $x = \cos\theta$.

assumes.text: The integral over $\kvarphi$, $\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(M-M')\kvarphi}\,d\kvarphi$, is zero unless $M = M'$.

steps.cap: So $\Delta M = 0$ is part of the rigid rotator selection rule.

nodes.note: The book calls this the integral over $f$; it is the integral over $\phi$.

assumes.text: Associated Legendre functions of the same $|M|$ are orthogonal: $\int_{-1}^{1}P_{J'}^{|M|}(x)P_{J''}^{|M|}(x)\,dx = 0$ unless $J' = J''$.

steps.cap: Substituting into the integral one obtains an integral which will vanish unless $J' = J + 1$ or $J' = J - 1$: each term is an overlap of two functions of the same $|M|$.

nodes.note: The book prints the second coefficient of the recurrence as $(J - |M|)$, twice, and writes $P_{J}^{|M]}$; the coefficient is $(J + |M|)$. Which integrals vanish does not depend on it.
